title: Arctic active layers in 2010-2024 were 7-8% deeper than a 1990-2009 thaw-index model predicted at 69 CALM sites; thaw of the previous five summers explains one third to one half of the excess
abstract: We tested a thaw-index (Stefan-type) model of end-of-season active-layer thickness (ALT) with the Circumpolar Active Layer Monitoring (CALM) table, 1990-2024, and Berkeley Earth (BE) and CRU TS 4.09 air temperature. The plan was written before the main tests. For 101 sites at 60 N or more (2,375 site-years), per-site fits of ALT on the square root of April-September thaw degree days for 1990-2009 under-predicted 2010-2024 ALT at 87% of 69 sites. The median residual was +7.8% of the mean ALT (95% CI +4.5 to +9.4, BE) and +7.3% (+5.0 to +9.1, CRU). The models predicted only 15-21% of the summed deepening. ALT kept a memory of earlier years: with site trends, a +1 SD warmer previous summer gave +0.84 cm (CI +0.60 to +1.08), against 2.3 cm for the same summer, and a colder preceding winter gave -0.6 to -0.8 cm. Residual lag-1 autocorrelation was +0.21 to +0.24 (null -0.09). After the largest 10% of ALT residuals, the excess was +0.24 site SD one year later, +0.14 to +0.19 two years later and zero after three years. Post hoc, lags 1-5 of the thaw index all had positive coefficients, also with quadratic site trends, without borehole sites and with CRU. Adding the mean thaw of the previous five summers raised the predicted share of the deepening to 35-42% and reduced the median residual to +4.4 to +5.5%. Two Alaska Interior thaw-tube sites with probable talik formation and six Swiss boreholes deepened much more than predicted. Limitations: gridded air temperature at 0.5-1 degree, monthly indices, no snow, soil moisture or subsidence data, post hoc lag models, and an unbalanced network. About half of the 2010-2024 deepening stays unexplained by air temperature.
